sense: money paid for a house or flat

evidence: Caes. BC 3.21.1: mercēdēs habitātiōnum annuās conductōribus dōnāvit
Cic. Att. 12.32.2: mercēdēs Argīlētī et Aventīnī, the rents from (his houses in) the Argiletum and on the Aventine
Traupman 370: mercēdem huic cellae dare, to pay the rent for this room
terms.comment: A house’s pay, as wages are a worker’s: mercēdēs habitātiōnum, the rents of dwellings. Cicero meant his son’s allowance at Athens to come out of the rents of two houses (Att. 12.32.2).

evidence: Suet. Ner. 44.2: pēnsiōnem annuam, a year’s rent
Juv. 9.63: pēnsiō clāmat, the rent cries out
terms.comment: In Cicero a payment or instalment (see pay in instalments); rent in Suetonius and Juvenal (Lewis & Short). Not a pension (see pension).

evidence: Cic. Cael. 17: sūmptus ūnīus generis objectus est, habitātiōnis
Suet. Jul. 38.2: annuam etiam habitātiōnem … remīsit, he let them off a year’s rent
terms.comment: What one pays for a dwelling: Caelius, said his accusers, lived at thirty thousand, trīgintā mīlibus habitāre (Cic. Cael. 17).

phrases.latin: Sūmptus ūnīus generis objectus est, habitātiōnis; trīgintā mīlibus dīxistis eum habitāre. Nunc dēmum intellegō P. Clōdī īnsulam esse vēnālem, cujus hic in aediculīs habitat decem, ut opīnor, mīlibus.
phrases.english: Only one kind of spending has been laid against him, his rent: you said he paid thirty thousand. Now at last I understand that Publius Clodius’s block of flats is up for sale: he lives in a little flat in it for ten thousand, I believe.

phrases.latin: ūnam, quā mercēdēs habitātiōnum annuās conductōribus dōnāvit
phrases.english: one (law), by which he let tenants off a year’s rent
to pay the rent for this room

sources: Lewis & Short: merces · Lewis & Short: pensio · Lewis & Short: habitatio
